notes.meaning: Abraham is about 140 years old, and God has blessed him richly in every area of life. Knowing his life on earth is drawing to a close, he wants to see Isaac married so God's covenant promises can continue. God's lifelong faithfulness gives His people confidence that He will guide their families into the future.

Abraham calls his oldest and most trusted servant, who is likely Eliezer. He asks him to put his hand under Abraham's thigh to make a solemn oath, which is a serious promise made before God. In that culture, this ancient act was a formal pledge of loyalty and showed deep respect for God's covenant.

Abraham makes the servant swear by the Lord, the Ruler of heaven and earth, not to find a wife for Isaac among the local Canaanites. The Canaanites worshiped idols and were headed for God's judgment, so marrying them would pull Isaac away from the true faith. Marriage choices should always protect a family's devotion to God.

Instead, Abraham directs his servant to travel back to Abraham's homeland and relatives in Mesopotamia to find a bride. Even though that distant family had flaws, they still knew something of the true God and belonged to Abraham's own people. God's promises were meant to pass down through a family that honored Him.

The servant asks a practical question before making the promise: what if the woman refuses to leave her home and move to Canaan? He asks whether he should then take Isaac back to Abraham's old country instead. The servant wants to understand the exact terms of the oath so he will not break his word.

Abraham firmly warns the servant never to take Isaac back to that land. Isaac was the heir of God's promise, and leaving Canaan would mean abandoning the land God had pledged to give them. Trusting God means refusing to go backward into old ways.

Abraham reassures his servant that the God of heaven will send His angel ahead of him to make the journey successful. God had called Abraham out of his homeland and promised this new land to his children, so Abraham trusted God to provide the right wife. God always provides the help needed to carry out what He has promised.

Abraham explains that if the woman refuses to follow, the servant is completely free from the oath. Even so, he repeats that Isaac must never be taken back there under any circumstances. Abraham preferred that his son wait rather than give up his calling from God.

The servant agrees, places his hand under Abraham's thigh, and takes the solemn oath. He commits himself fully to carry out his master's wishes in the fear of God. A faithful helper treats a master's spiritual priorities as his own.

The servant sets out with ten camels loaded with choice gifts and supplies, heading for the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia. Having ten camels and valuable goods showed Abraham's great wealth and honored his family before the prospective bride. Doing God's work with care often involves good planning and generous preparation.

Arriving near the town toward evening, the servant has the camels kneel down to rest by a well outside the city. In those days, evening was the customary time for women to come draw water for their households. The servant placed himself where he was most likely to meet the people of the town.

The servant stops to pray, asking the God of Abraham to grant him success that day and show loving-kindness to his master. He does not ask for his own glory, but for Abraham's sake and for God's covenant promise. It is always wise to bring our specific daily tasks to God in prayer.

Standing by the spring as the young women come out with their water jars, the servant watches and waits. He knows human wisdom alone cannot find the right wife for Isaac among all the townspeople. He puts himself in the place of duty while depending entirely on the Lord.

The servant asks God for a clear sign: he will ask a girl for a drink, and if she offers to water his ten camels too, she will be God's chosen bride. This was a test of her kindness, humility, and willingness to work hard for a tired stranger. True godliness often shows itself in generous everyday service.

Before he even finishes praying in his heart, Rebekah walks out carrying a water jar on her shoulder. She is the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, matching the exact family Abraham sent him to find. God often hears and answers the prayers of His people before they even finish speaking.

Rebekah is described as very beautiful, pure, and unmarried. She walks down to the spring, fills her jar, and carries it back up, minding her own business without distraction. Her modest behavior and quiet hard work show her fine character.

The servant runs to meet her and politely asks for just a little sip of water from her jar. He asks for only a small drink so he can see how she responds to a stranger's simple need. Faithful prayer does not keep a person from taking practical action.

Rebekah answers with great respect, calling him 'my lord,' and quickly lowers her heavy jar into her hands to give him a drink. Her cheerful and swift hospitality reveals a kind heart toward a weary traveler. Common courtesy can be a doorway through which God does great things.

After giving him a drink, Rebekah offers to draw water for all ten of his camels until they have had enough. Camels drink a huge amount of water after a long journey, so this was an extraordinary offer that meant exhausting labor. Her generous spirit went far beyond ordinary manners.

Rebekah quickly empties her jar into the watering trough and runs back and forth to the well until all ten camels are satisfied. Her actions match the exact sign the servant had requested in his prayer. A truly willing heart proves itself by hard work.

The servant watches her in silence, wondering whether the Lord has truly made his journey successful. He is amazed at how quickly and completely God is answering his prayer, yet he waits for full confirmation. When God works in our lives, quiet observation and wonder are often the right response.

When the camels finish drinking, the servant takes out a gold nose-ring and two gold bracelets to give to Rebekah. These valuable gifts rewarded her kindness and showed the wealth of the household she might join. God rewards kindness in ways that can take us completely by surprise.
